items.stem: Briefly explain why f(x) = x² with domain x ∈ ℝ has no inverse function, and how the domain can be restricted so that it does.
items.answer: Two inputs (e.g. ±2) give the same output, so the reverse mapping is not a function (fails the horizontal line test); restricting to x ≥ 0 makes it one-to-one.

items.stem: A student claims: "Because a linear model fits data from 0 to 10 years, it can be used to predict the value after 50 years." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Extrapolating far outside the data range is unreliable; the rate of change may not stay constant.
items.markingKey: Extrapolating far outside the data range is unreliable; the rate of change may not stay constant. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A water company in Boston charges a fixed 9 USD per month, 1.52 USD per m³ for the first 10 m³, and 2.85 USD per m³ for any further water. (a) Write down a piecewise function for the cost. (b) Show that the function is continuous at 10. (c) A customer pays 52.70 USD. Find the amount of water used. (d) Find the average cost per unit for this customer and explain why it differs from the gradient of the final piece.
items.markingKey: (a) A2. (b) R1 both pieces give 24.20 at the boundary. (c) set the second piece equal to 52.70 (M1) ⇒ 20 (A1). (d) 52.70 ÷ 20 = 2.64 (A1); R1 the average includes the cheaper/fixed parts, whereas the gradient is the marginal rate.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The change in the output per unit change in the input; for a linear model, its gradient, with units"?
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of rate of change.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The value of y where a graph crosses the y-axis, i.e. at x = 0"?
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of y-intercept.

items.stem: Define the term "inverse function".
items.answer: Denoted f⁻¹, the function that reverses f, so that f⁻¹(f(x)) = x; its graph is the reflection of y = f(x) in y = x
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: denoted f⁻¹, the function that reverses f, so that f⁻¹(f(x)) = x; its graph is the reflection of y = f(x) in y = x. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the gradients of two perpendicular lines (neither vertical) multiply to −1.
items.answer: Rotating a line by 90° turns a run of 1 and rise of m into a run of −m and rise of 1, so the new gradient is −1/m.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rotating a line by 90° turns a run of 1 and rise of m into a run of −m and rise of 1, so the new gradient is −1/m. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the domain of a function in a real-life model is often smaller than the set of all real numbers.
items.answer: Inputs such as time, length or number of items must be non-negative or whole numbers, and the model may only be valid for a limited range.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Inputs such as time, length or number of items must be non-negative or whole numbers, and the model may only be valid for a limited range. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Two tariffs for a bike-hire scheme: Plan A costs 70 USD per month plus 1.72 USD per unit; Plan B costs 4 USD per month plus 3.20 USD per unit (units: hours). items.answer: (a) C_A = 1.72x + 70, C_B = 3.20x + 4 (b) x = 44.6 (c) cost per extra unit (d) see key

items.stem: "f⁻¹(x) means 1/f(x)." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: f⁻¹ denotes the inverse function, which undoes f; 1/f(x) is the reciprocal, written (f(x))⁻¹.
